Revised assessment incorporating economic-finance literature:
- Elevated inflation alongside tight labor markets is consistent with New Keynesian models linking prices to real marginal costs and sticky prices (e.g., Galí). COVID-related supply and demand imbalances and China’s lockdowns represent supply-chain shocks, while the Ukraine-driven energy price shock historically depresses growth and lifts inflation in VAR evidence on oil shocks, raising near-term stagflation risk.
- The FOMC’s rate hike and the start of balance-sheet reduction align with Taylor-rule-style responses and the Bernanke–Mihov view of the federal funds rate as the key policy instrument. Higher policy rates typically reduce investment (neoclassical q/IS channels) and, via credit-market frictions, can amplify real effects (Gertler et al.), implying some cooling ahead.
- QT and money-market settings (IOER, ON RRP) are consistent with the modern operating framework; reserve balance shrinkage can modestly tighten financial conditions via term premia and MBS markets.
- Credible tightening and inflation-forecast–based communication (Svensson and Woodford) help anchor expectations and mitigate longer-run costs from inflation bias, partially offsetting near-term growth risks.

Net tone: more negative than before due to heightened supply shocks and tightening, but tempered by strong household spending, business investment, and robust job gains.
